```{r}
calc_inc <- function(ghg_vector, year_vector, since) {
  if (length(ghg_vector) != length(year_vector)) {
    stop("ghg and years must be the same length", call. = FALSE)
  }
  
  ghg_now <- ghg_vector[which.max(year_vector)]
  ghg_then <- ghg_vector[year_vector == since]
  
  perc <- ((ghg_now/ghg_then) - 1)*100
  perc
}

two_years_ago = calc_inc(bc_ghg_sum$ghg_estimate, bc_ghg_sum$year, max(bc_ghg_sum$year)-2)

net_2007 <- bc_ghg_sum$ghg_estimate[bc_ghg_sum$year==2007]
```

-   **Greenhouse gas emissions warm the global atmosphere and cause our climate to change.** Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is a key component to limiting the increase in global average temperature and the resulting climate changes.

-   **A rebound in greenhouse gas emissions was observed in 2021 and continued into 2022, from the low 2020 levels brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic.** This was primarily driven by an increase in emissions from road and off-road transportation, railways, as well as domestic aviation and marine transportation. 

-   **Total greenhouse gas emissions in `r max_ghg_yr` in B.C. were `r round(ghg_est_MtCO2e,1)` million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO~2~e).** This is a `r abs(round(previous_year,1))`% `r ifelse(previous_year > 0, 'increase', 'decrease')` in gross emissions since `r max_ghg_yr - 1`, a `r abs(round(two_years_ago,1))`% `r ifelse(two_years_ago > 0, 'increase', 'decrease')` in gross emissions since `r max_ghg_yr - 2`, and a `r abs(round(baseline_year,1))`% `r ifelse(baseline_year > 0, "increase", "decrease")` in gross emissions since 2007---the Government of British Columbia's baseline year for assessing reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.

<!-- B.C.'s outlook suggests that emissions are likely to rebound to a degree in 2021 as economic activity (including air travel and road transportation) returns to normal (see page 10 of [B.C.'s 2023 Climate Change Accountability Report](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/climate-change/action/cleanbc/2023_climate_change_accountability_report.pdf)^1^). -->

-   **B.C. applies emissions reductions from forest management carbon offsets to emission totals each year to determine net greenhouse gas emissions and progress to its official legislated targets.** In 2022, carbon offsets totaled `r round(offset_val_Mtco2e,1)` Mt CO~2~e, bringing net greenhouse gas emissions down to `r round((ghg_est_MtCO2e - offset_val_Mtco2e),1)` Mt CO~2~e, `r round(((net_2007 - (ghg_est_MtCO2e - offset_val_Mtco2e))/net_2007)*100,1)`% below 2007 levels. Figures and calculations presented in this indicator use gross totals from the [British Columbia Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventory (`r max_ghg_yr`)](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/climate-change/data/provincial-inventory)^1^ and do not account for any emission reductions from offset projects.

-   **B.C. has set targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions over the next 30 years.** The targets are 40% reduction by 2030, 60% reduction by 2040 and 80% reduction by 2050, compared to 2007 levels. To keep B.C. on track, an interim target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 16% from 2007 levels by 2025 was also set^2^.

-   **Greenhouse gas emissions intensity of the economy continues to fall.** Greenhouse gas emissions per million dollars of GDP have been in decline since 1990 with the trend accelerating after 2001. The trend in emissions per person is less consistent, but has been downward for most of the last 20 years.

-   **Different gases make up the total greenhouse gas emissions reported over time.** The gases released in 2022 were carbon dioxide (`r percent_CO2`% of total emissions), methane (`r percent_CH4`%), nitrous oxide (`r percent_N2O`%), hydrofluorocarbons (`r percent_HFCs`%), and perfluorocarbons (`r percent_PFCs`%). 

-   **The transportation sector and oil and gas sector produce the most greenhouse gas emissions in B.C.** Major transportation-related sources of greenhouse gas emissions include road and off-road transportation. The major oil and gas source is fuel use.

\newpage

## Greenhouse Gas Emissions in British Columbia

-   In `r max_ghg_yr`, gross greenhouse gas emissions in B.C. were `r abs(round(baseline_year,1))`% `r ifelse(baseline_year > 0, "higher", "lower")` than the 2007 baseline year.


-   Per capita and greenhouse gas intensities are based on gross emissions totals. Values reported differ from those used in the [B.C.'s 2023 Climate Change Accountability Report](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/climate-change/action/cleanbc/2023_climate_change_accountability_report.pdf)^2^, which uses net emissions totals to calculate corresponding intensities.\vspace{.2cm}

\vspace{.2cm}

-   Overall, the greenhouse gases produced per person in B.C. were less in 2022 than in the 2007 baseline year. Much of the decrease in 2020 is likely due to the COVID-19 pandemic, with a rebound in greenhouse gas emissions per person observed since 2021. This rebound was expected as people and business returned to pre-pandemic activities after the COVID-19 public-health restrictions were lifted.

## Emissions by Greenhouse Gas

-   There are 7 greenhouse gases monitored in B.C. The gases are carbon dioxide (CO~2~), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), methane (CH~4~), nitrous oxide (N~2~O), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur hexafluoride (SF~6~), and nitrogen trifluoride (NF~3~).  

-   Greenhouse gases have different [Global Warming Potential](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/climate-change/greenhouse-gas-emissions/quantification-guidance/global-warming-potentials.html)^3^ (GWP). The GWP determines how much a gas traps heat in the atmosphere. For example, methane traps 25 times more heat than carbon dioxide, while sulphur hexafluoride traps 22,880 times more heat than carbon dioxide. To combine different gases for an overall emissions total, the emission values of each gas are converted to CO~2~ equivalent in all of the figures and data in this indicator ([British Columbia Greenhouse Gas Provincial Inventory Methodology](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/climate-change/data/provincial-inventory/2021/provincial_inventory_of_greenhouse_gas_emissions_1990-2021_-_methodology_report.pdf)^4^).

- The relative contribution of each greenhouse gas emitted in 2022 was CO~2~  at `r percent_CO2`%, CH~4~ at `r percent_CH4`%, N~2~O at `r percent_N2O`%, HFCs at `r percent_HFCs`%, PFCs at `r percent_PFCs`%, and SF~6~ at `r percent_SF6`%. There have been no recorded emissions of NF~3~ in B.C. to date.

## How have emissions of different greenhouse gases changed over time? 

- The amount of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted annually by each greenhouse gas was compared to 1990 levels. CO~2~ emissions have fluctuated over time. CH~4~ emissions have also varied since 1990 but have consistently declined since 2013. 

- HFC emissions have gradually increased since 1990, peaking in 2020.

- N~2~O and SF~6~ emissions have changed very little since 1990. SF~6~ emissions have been at or near 0 MtCO~2~e since 2011. 

- PFC emissions have varied from year to year but have generally declined since 1998 and are below 1990 emissions.

## Greenhouse Gas Emissions by Sector

-   Greenhouse gas emissions are sorted into the following sectors: transportation, other industry, buildings and communities as well as oil and gas. 

-   B.C. has set targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions in each sector by 2030. The targets are `r round(clean_bc_2030_transport,1)` Mt CO~2~e for transportation sector, `r round(clean_bc_2030_Other_industry,1)` Mt CO~2~e for other industry sector, `r round(clean_bc_2030_Buildings_Communities,1)` Mt CO~2~e for buildings and communities sector, and `r round(clean_bc_2030_Oils_Gas,1)` Mt CO~2~e for oil and gas sector.

-   By looking at the greenhouse gas emissions across the different sectors, we can see where the majority of B.C.'s emissions are coming from, as well as the trends in emissions from those sectors.

-   The transportation sector produces the largest amount of greenhouse gas emissions in British Columbia. This sector includes transportation emissions other than those from pipelines.

-   The other industry sector produces a large amount of greenhouse gas emissions in British Columbia. This sector includes: 
    -   Combustion, fugitive, and process emissions from non-oil and gas industry
    -   Emissions from construction and agriculture

## How have greenhouse gas emissions changed within sectors?

-   The amount of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted annually by each sector was compared to 1990 levels. The transportation sector had the largest increase in annual emissions of any sector over the past three decades. The oil and gas sector also had consistent increases in annual emissions, with levels peaking from 2008 to 2014.

-   Emissions from the transportation sector in `r max_ghg_yr` `r ifelse(previous_year > 0, 'increased', 'decreased')` `r abs(round(previous_year,1))`% from `r max_ghg_yr - 1` levels but remained `r abs(round(three_year,1))`% lower than `r max_ghg_yr - 3` levels. The rebound in transportation emissions in `r max_ghg_yr` is likely due to fewer COVID-19 travel restrictions.

-   Emissions from the buildings and communities sector declined since 1990 and have fluctuated over the past decade.

-   Emissions from the other industry sectors declined from 2001 to 2008.

-   Each sector was broken down into more specific categories where available. This information is provided below.

## Methods

The [British Columbia Greenhouse Gas Provincial Inventory Methodology](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/climate-change/data/provincial-inventory/2021/provincial_inventory_of_greenhouse_gas_emissions_1990-2021_-_methodology_report.pdf)^4^ describes the methodologies and data sources used in preparing B.C.'s greenhouse gas emissions inventory. Currently, most of the Provincial Inventory data and methods come from [Canada's National Inventory Report (NIR)](http://www.publications.gc.ca/site/eng/9.506002/publication.html)^5^. Any deviations from the NIR methodology or categorization are described in detail in the B.C. Provincial Inventory Methodology^4^. Additional information is also available in the [British Columbia Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventory (2021)](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/climate-change/data/provincial-inventory)^1^.

 British Columbia population estimates ([Table: 17-10-0005-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1710000501)) and gross domestic product ([Table: 36-10-0222-01](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=3610022201)) data were sourced from [Statistics Canada](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/eng/start). Gross domestic product (GDP) is calculated using expenditure-based GDP and reported in millions of chained 2017 dollars. 
 
The Sector data in this indicator is from the 'Economic Sector' described on Page 10 of the [B.C.'s 2023 Climate Change Accountability Report](https://www2.gov.bc.ca/assets/gov/environment/climate-change/action/cleanbc/2023_climate_change_accountability_report.pdf)^2^. 

The [**R**](http://www.r-project.org) code for repeating the analysis and data visualizations presented on this page is [available on GitHub](https://github.com/bcgov/ghg-emissions-indicator).
